steps.body: A HALF-period slide flips a wave upside down: **sin(x + π) = −sin x** and **cos(x + π) = −cos x**. So reflection (the outside minus, recall) and a π-slide are the SAME motion for sinusoids — one graph can wear rules that look wildly different.

predict.prompt: Slide x forward by HALF a period — add π. What happens to the point's two coordinates, cos and sin?

options.label: Both flip sign — the point jumps to the far side of the circle
Only sine flips — cosine is even, it never changes
Neither — a slide moves the wave, not its values

predict.reveal: Adding π sends the point to its antipode, straight through the center — so BOTH coordinates flip: sin(x + π) = −sin x and cos(x + π) = −cos x. (“Only sine flips” is a different identity: that one belongs to −x, not to x + π.)

widget.prompt: The tracked point sits at x + 180°. Pick the formula that computes it from cos x and sin x without ever letting go, then land x on 90° — where the flip becomes sin(3π/2).

ghostChoices.label: (cos x + cos 180°, sin x + sin 180°) — add the half-turn to each coordinate
ghostChoices.feedback: Watch the readout: this point slides to (cos x − 1, sin x) and leaves the circle — coordinates do not add under a rotation. The half-turn acts on the ANGLE, and through the angle it flips both coordinates at once.

widget.successFeedback: Glued at every x — the point at x + 180° is the antipode, so both coordinates flip together. At x = 90° that reads sin(3π/2) = −sin(π/2) = −1, the very number the next step asks you to write down. One wave, two names, half a period apart.
widget.lowFeedback: Formula's right — keep dragging to 90°, where the flip becomes the value the lesson opened with.
widget.highFeedback: Past 90° — ease back to the angle whose half-period partner is 3π/2.

widget.prompt: Evaluate sin(π/2 + π) = sin(3π/2). It should equal −sin(π/2). What is it?

commonErrors.feedback: sin(3π/2) = −1 (unit circle bottom): the π-slide turned the peak value 1 into −1.
3π/2 is the circle's BOTTOM, not a midline crossing: sin(3π/2) = −1.

explanationVariants: −sin x equals sin(x + π): the outside minus IS a half-period slide.
Both rules start at the midline heading DOWN; test x = π/2: both give −1.

widget.prompt: Which rule draws the SAME graph as y = −sin x?

options.label: y = sin(x + π)
options.feedback: Right — a π-slide flips sine: sin(x + π) = −sin x at every x.

options.label: y = sin(x + π/2)
options.feedback: That's COSINE (quarter-period slide), which starts at a PEAK — but −sin starts at the midline going down.

options.label: y = sin(−x + π/2)
options.feedback: sin(π/2 − x) = cos x — the peak-starter again. −sin x needs the half-period slide: sin(x + π).

explanationVariants: −cos x = cos(x − π) (or x + π — half a period either way): trough at 0 instead of a peak.

widget.prompt: y = −cos x is the same graph as:

options.label: y = cos(x − π)
options.feedback: Right — slide cosine half a period and its peak becomes a trough at 0: exactly −cos x.

options.label: y = cos(x − π/2)
options.feedback: A QUARTER slide gives sin x (midline start), not the trough-start of −cos x.

options.label: y = cos(x) − π
options.feedback: Subtracting π OUTSIDE drops the midline by π — a vertical move, no flip. The flip needs the inside π-slide.

steps.body: Equivalence is testable: two rules name the same wave iff they agree on the **landmarks** — same midline, amplitude, period, and same value-and-direction at one x. Checking a single well-chosen point (plus the dials) beats expanding identities.

explanationVariants: At x = 0: 2 sin(x + π/2) gives 2·1 = 2, but 2 cos(x + π) gives 2·(−1) = −2 — opposite postures, NOT the same wave.
2 sin(x + π/2) = 2 cos x (peak at 0); 2 cos(x + π) = −2 cos x (trough at 0): negatives of each other.

widget.prompt: A student claims 2 sin(x + π/2) and 2 cos(x + π) draw the same graph. Check x = 0:

options.label: They give 2 and −2 — different graphs (they're reflections)
options.feedback: Right — one is 2 cos x, the other −2 cos x: one test point exposes the flip.

options.label: Both give 2 — same graph
options.feedback: cos(0 + π) = cos π = −1, so the second rule gives −2 at x = 0.

options.label: Both give 0 — same graph
options.feedback: Neither is 0 at x = 0: sin(π/2) = 1 and cos(π) = −1, giving 2 and −2.

explanationVariants: cos(x − π/2) = sin x, and sin(x + 2π) = sin x (full period changes nothing). But sin(x − π) = −sin x — the flipped wave, the odd one out.
Test x = π/2: sin gives 1; cos(π/2 − π/2) = cos 0 = 1 ✓; sin(π/2 + 2π) = 1 ✓; sin(π/2 − π) = sin(−π/2) = −1 ✗.
hints: Test each rule at one convenient x, like π/2, against sin(π/2) = 1.
Full-period slides (±2π) never change a wave.
sin(x − π) is a HALF-period slide — what does that do?

widget.prompt: Which rule is NOT equivalent to y = sin x?

options.label: y = sin(x − π)
options.feedback: Right — half-period slide = flip: sin(x − π) = −sin x. At π/2 it gives −1, not 1.

options.label: y = cos(x − π/2)
options.feedback: That IS sine (the twin identity): at π/2 it gives cos 0 = 1 ✓.

options.label: y = sin(x + 2π)
options.feedback: A full-period slide is invisible — identical wave: at π/2 it gives 1 ✓.

takeaways: π-slide = reflection: sin(x + π) = −sin x, cos(x ± π) = −cos x.
Audit equivalences with the dials plus one test point.
steps.teaser: Next chapter: the wave that ISN'T a wave — tangent and its asymptote fence.

concept.body: To test whether two rules draw the same graph: compare midline, amplitude, period — then evaluate both at one x. Any disagreement ends it.

explanationVariants: cos(0 + π) = −1: the rule cos(x + π) starts at a TROUGH, value −1.

widget.prompt: What is cos(x + π) at x = 0?

commonErrors.feedback: cos(0) = 1, but the argument is 0 + π: cos π = −1 — the upside-down start.
π is the circle's LEFT point (−1, 0): cosine reads −1 there.
